To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) the amino-terminal end and the interdomain linker of a membrane protein determine the topology of the protein in the membrane, (b) circularly permuted domains of the same protein can have similar activities, and (c) the phosphorylation domain of the glucose transporter can not be substituted for in the transport reaction
a domain swap of IICBGlc by circular permutation leads to a functional transport system and that the IIC and IIB domains are two cooperative units in the transport cycle.

circular permutation and domain swapping of the glucose transporter are possible, that the amino-terminal domain of the IIC domain must be cytoplasmic, that the phosphorylation domain IIB cannot be replaced by glucokinase, and that transmembrane transport of glucose is conformationally coupled with the phosphorylation/de-phosphorylation cycle in the IIB domain.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the design of the bacterial PTS transporters and the mechanism of substrate translocation and phosphorylation.
the design and evolution of the PTS transporters.
the functional analysis of the membrane-spanning domain of the glucose transporter of Escherichius coli.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the circularly permutable domain order of the glucose transporter is a consequence of the evolutionary history of the transporter, and the domain order in IIBCGlc is not an optimal design.
circular permutation and domain swap can rapidly lead to functional protein, but not necessarily to a functional protein complex.
the IIC domain is a substrate binding and a translocation unit that is independent of IIA and IIA, but dependent on IIB, which is an ATP-independent phosphorylation/dephophosphorylation unit.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the IIC and IIB domains can be exchanged by a single DNA rearrangement, but the resulting circularly permuted protein is not a glucokinase.

the IIC domain is an autonomous membrane protein with a substrate-binding site, that it is inserted into the membrane independently from its amino-terminal end and that it is a substrate-binding unit of a functional protein complex.
a domain swap in a membrane transporter can rapidly lead to an active enzyme, but that a functional domain cannot easily be replaced by an enzyme with a different catalytic mechanism.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the domain structure of IICBGlc can be altered without losing transport activity.
circular permutation of domains in proteins is a powerful approach to study the functional importance of domain order and to identify functional elements in proteins.
the PTS is a good model for studying the modular assembly of proteins, and that circularly permuted domains are not a rare event in evolution.
